name: Farm Accounting and Investment Management
objectives: Given a list of one enterprise's costs for a season and its yield, sort the costs into fixed and variable and calculate the cost to produce one kg, bag, litre or egg, with every cost in the right group and the cost per unit correct to the nearest whole unit of money

Using a notebook or a phone spreadsheet, record every farm expense for one month by date, category and enterprise, and total it by category, with no missing days and totals that match your cash and mobile money records

Given expected money in and out for each month of a year, build a monthly cash-flow plan with opening and closing balances and mark the shortfall months, with each closing balance carried to the next month and at least one action planned for every shortfall month

Given total costs, expected yield and a buyer's price, calculate the break-even price and break-even yield and decide whether the offer covers your costs, correct to the nearest whole unit of money or unit of yield

Given the cost of an investment and the extra income and costs it should bring, calculate its payback period and simple return and write a decision with your reasons, with correct numbers and at least two risks checked (life of the item, loan cost or weaker yields)

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Fixed and variable costs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort one enterprise's costs into fixed and variable, including the yearly cost of tools and buildings.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of one enterprise's costs for a season and its yield, you will sort the costs into fixed and variable and calculate the cost to produce one kg, bag, litre or egg, with every cost in the right group and the cost per unit correct to the nearest whole unit of money.
Variable costs go up or down with how much you produce: seed, fertilizer, feed, day labour, vet services, bags, fuel and transport. If you plant half the land or keep half the birds, these costs fall.
Fixed costs stay about the same whatever you produce in the season: land rent, a permanent worker's wage, a water licence, insurance, and the wearing out of tools, pumps, sheds and fences. That wearing out is called depreciation. A simple way to work it out: (price paid - value left at the end) / years it will last. Example (made-up numbers in Kenya shillings): a knapsack sprayer costs 6,000, will last 5 years and be worth nothing at the end, so it costs the farm 1,200 a year.
If a tool or a building serves several enterprises, share its yearly cost between them, for example by the land or the time each uses. Count your family's labour too, at the local day rate, so you see the true cost of your time.
Step by step:
- Choose one enterprise, such as maize, tilapia or a dairy cow.
- List every cost for one season or one year.
- Mark each one V (variable: changes with how much you produce) or F (fixed: stays the same).
- For tools, pumps and buildings, work out depreciation: (price - value left) / years of life.
- Share fixed costs between enterprises that use the same thing.
Words to know:
- Variable cost: a cost that rises or falls with how much you produce, such as seed or feed.
- Fixed cost: a cost that stays about the same whatever you produce in the season, such as land rent.
- Depreciation: the part of a tool's or building's price that is used up each year as it wears out.
- Enterprise: one activity on the farm, such as maize, poultry or dairy.
Try it now: Pick one enterprise on your farm. List at least eight costs from the last season, mark each V or F, and work out the yearly depreciation of one tool or building you use for it.
You can now sort an enterprise's costs into fixed and variable and work out the yearly cost of your tools and buildings.

check.q: Which of these is a variable cost for a poultry enterprise?
options: The yearly wear on the poultry house
Rent for the plot the house stands on
check.why: Feed rises and falls with how many birds you keep, so it is variable.

check.q: A pump costs 50,000, will last 10 years and be worth 0 at the end. Its depreciation is:

lessons.title: Lesson 2: What it costs to produce one kg, bag or litre
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost to produce one kg, bag, litre or egg for one enterprise.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of one enterprise's costs for a season and its yield, you will sort the costs into fixed and variable and calculate the cost to produce one kg, bag, litre or egg, with every cost in the right group and the cost per unit correct to the nearest whole unit of money.
Cost per unit = total cost for the period / units produced in that period. Total cost is variable costs plus the share of fixed costs that belongs to this enterprise. The unit is how you sell: a kg of tomatoes, a 100 kg bag of maize, a litre of milk, a tray of eggs, a kg of tilapia.
Example (made-up numbers in Kenya shillings), one dairy cow for one month: feed 9,500, vet and breeding services 1,000, labour 3,000, share of fixed costs (shed, chaff cutter, water) 1,500. Total 15,000. The cow gave 300 litres. Cost per litre = 15,000 / 300 = 50 shillings. If the milk buyer pays less than 50, every litre loses money.
Example (made-up numbers in naira), one hectare of maize in Nigeria: variable costs 600,000, share of fixed costs 150,000, total 750,000, harvest 30 bags of 100 kg. Cost per bag = 750,000 / 30 = 25,000, which is 250 naira per kg. Work it out every season: when yields fall or input prices rise, the cost per unit rises too.
Step by step:
- Choose the unit you sell in: kg, bag, litre, egg or tray.
- Add the variable costs for the period.
- Add this enterprise's share of fixed costs.
- Count the units produced in the same period.
- Cost per unit = total cost / units produced.
- Compare it with the price buyers pay.
Words to know:
- Cost per unit: what it costs you to produce one kg, bag, litre or egg: total cost divided by units produced.
- Unit: the amount you sell in, such as a kg, a 100 kg bag or a litre.
Try it now: Use the costs from Lesson 1. Add them up, divide by the units you produced, and write your cost per kg, bag, litre or egg. Then write the last price a buyer offered you next to it.
You can now calculate the cost to produce one unit of what you sell and compare it with the price you are offered.

check.q: Total cost for a tomato plot is 40,000 and it produced 800 kg. What is the cost per kg?
Your yield falls but your costs stay the same. What happens to your cost per unit?
check.why: The same cost divided by fewer units gives a higher cost for each unit.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: An expense tracker you can keep
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up an expense tracker and record every farm expense for a month.
This lesson builds toward: Using a notebook or a phone spreadsheet, you will record every farm expense for one month by date, category and enterprise, and total it by category, with no missing days and totals that match your cash and mobile money records.
An expense tracker is a list of every farm payment with the same columns each time: date, what you bought, category (seed, fertilizer, feed, labour, vet, fuel, transport, repairs, rent), which enterprise, F or V, amount, how you paid (cash or mobile money) and whether you kept a receipt.
Write each expense the same day. At the end of the month, add up each category and each enterprise. You will quickly see where the money goes. Example (made-up numbers in Ghana cedis), a layer farm in one month: feed 4,200, labour 1,200, vet and vaccines 400, transport 300, repairs 150, total 6,250. Feed is two thirds of the cost, so the best savings will come from feed.
A notebook works well. On a phone, a free spreadsheet such as Google Sheets or Microsoft Excel can add up each category for you with the SUMIF formula. Check the tracker against your cash and mobile money statements every week, so nothing is missed.
Step by step:
- Make the columns: date, item, category, enterprise, F or V, amount, paid by, receipt.
- Write each expense the same day.
- Every week, check it against your cash and mobile money statement.
- At month end, total each category and each enterprise.
- Find the biggest category and one way to cut it.
Words to know:
- Expense tracker: a list of every farm payment with the same columns, so you can add it up by category.
- Category: a group of similar costs, such as feed, labour or transport.
- Receipt: a paper or message that proves you paid.
Try it now: Set up your tracker today with all eight columns. Fill in every farm expense from the last seven days using your memory, receipts and mobile money statement, then total them by category.
You can now keep an expense tracker, total it by category and enterprise, and find where your money goes.

check.q: Why add a column for which enterprise each expense belongs to?
options: So you can see what each enterprise really costs
Because banks require it every day
So you do not need receipts
check.why: Totals by enterprise feed straight into the cost per unit for each one.

check.q: Your tracker total is lower than what left your mobile money wallet this month. What do you do?
options: Ignore it; small gaps do not matter
Delete the tracker and start again next year
Go through the statement and add the missing expenses
Add a made-up number to make them match
check.why: The statement shows what you really paid, so it helps you find and add missing entries.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: A monthly cash-flow plan with balances
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a 12-month cash-flow plan with opening and closing balances and mark the shortfall months.
This lesson builds toward: Given expected money in and out for each month of a year, you will build a monthly cash-flow plan with opening and closing balances and mark the shortfall months, with each closing balance carried to the next month and at least one action planned for every shortfall month.
A cash-flow plan shows, month by month, how much money you expect to have. For each month: opening balance (money you start with) + money in - money out = closing balance. The closing balance becomes next month's opening balance.
Example (made-up numbers in Ghana cedis), a maize and poultry farm. March: opening 3,000 + in 500 - out 2,000 = closing 1,500. April: opening 1,500 + in 500 - out 2,500 = closing -500. A minus closing balance is a shortfall: you will not be able to pay everything that month unless you plan.
For each shortfall month, plan an action before it comes: save from the last harvest, move a purchase to a later month, sell some produce in stages, add a small enterprise that earns in that month (eggs, vegetables, fish), arrange input credit, or agree a small loan in advance with repayments after harvest. Update the plan each month with what really happened.
Step by step:
- Make 12 month columns and four rows: opening, money in, money out, closing.
- Put the cash you have now as the first opening balance.
- Fill in expected money in and money out for each month.
- Closing = opening + in - out; carry it to next month's opening.
- Circle every minus closing balance.
- Write one action for each circled month and update monthly.
Words to know:
- Opening balance: the money you have at the start of a month.
- Closing balance: the money you expect at the end of a month: opening + money in - money out.
- Shortfall: a month when money out is more than the money you have.
Try it now: Build your 12-month cash-flow plan starting with the cash you have today. Work out every closing balance, circle the shortfall months, and write one action for each.
You can now build a monthly cash-flow plan with running balances, spot shortfall months early and plan what to do about them.

check.q: Opening balance 2,000, money in 1,000, money out 2,500. What is the closing balance?
Your plan shows a shortfall in August. When should you plan what to do?
options: In August, when the bills arrive
Never; it will sort itself out
check.why: Planning early gives you time to save, move purchases or arrange credit on good terms.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The break-even price and yield
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Calculate the break-even price and break-even yield and use them to judge a buyer's offer.
This lesson builds toward: Given total costs, expected yield and a buyer's price, you will calculate the break-even price and break-even yield and decide whether the offer covers your costs, correct to the nearest whole unit of money or unit of yield.
Break-even is the point where income just covers total cost: no profit and no loss. Break-even price = total cost / expected yield. It is the lowest price you can accept without losing money. Break-even yield = total cost / price you expect. It is the smallest harvest that covers your costs at that price.
Example (made-up numbers in naira), the maize hectare from Lesson 2: total cost 750,000, expected harvest 30 bags. Break-even price = 750,000 / 30 = 25,000 a bag. A buyer offers 28,000: you make 3,000 a bag, or 90,000 on 30 bags. Break-even yield at 28,000 = 750,000 / 28,000 = 26.8 bags, so you need at least 27 bags. If drought cuts your harvest to 25 bags, you lose money even at that price.
Use break-even before you plant (is this crop worth it at likely prices?) and when a buyer makes an offer (does it cover my costs?). The gap between the expected price and your break-even price is your safety margin: the bigger it is, the more a bad season or a price fall you can take.
Step by step:
- Add up total cost for the enterprise (variable + share of fixed).
- Break-even price = total cost / expected yield.
- Break-even yield = total cost / expected price.
- Compare with the buyer's offer and your likely yield.
- Write your safety margin: expected price - break-even price.
Words to know:
- Break-even: the point where income just covers total cost: no profit, no loss.
- Break-even price: the lowest price per unit that covers your costs: total cost / yield.
- Break-even yield: the smallest harvest that covers your costs at a given price: total cost / price.
- Safety margin: how far the price or yield can fall before you make a loss.
Try it now: Use your enterprise's total cost and expected yield. Work out the break-even price and the break-even yield at today's price, and write your safety margin. Would you accept the last offer you got?
You can now calculate the break-even price and yield for an enterprise and use them to accept or refuse an offer.

check.q: Total cost 120,000, expected yield 40 bags. What is the break-even price?
Your break-even price for milk is 50 a litre. A buyer offers 45. What does this mean?
options: You make 5 profit on each litre
You lose about 5 on each litre unless you cut costs or find a better buyer
The offer is fair because it is close
Break-even does not matter for milk
check.why: A price below break-even means every litre sold loses money.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Judging an investment: payback and simple return
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the payback period and simple return of an investment and decide whether it makes sense.
This lesson builds toward: Given the cost of an investment and the extra income and costs it should bring, you will calculate its payback period and simple return and write a decision with your reasons, with correct numbers and at least two risks checked (life of the item, loan cost or weaker yields).
An investment is money spent now to earn more later: a solar pump, a greenhouse, a cold store, a pig house or more cows. First work out the extra net income per year: the extra money it brings in minus the extra running costs (fuel, repairs, feed, labour, replacement parts). Then: payback period = investment cost / extra net income per year. Simple return = extra net income per year / investment cost x 100.
Example (made-up numbers in Kenya shillings), a solar pump that allows a dry-season tomato crop: cost 120,000; extra income 55,000 a year minus extra costs 15,000 = 40,000 extra net income. Payback = 120,000 / 40,000 = 3 years. Simple return = 40,000 / 120,000 x 100 = about 33% a year. Example (made-up numbers in CFA francs), a greenhouse in Senegal: cost 3,000,000; extra net income 600,000 a year. Payback = 5 years; simple return = 20% a year.
Then check the risks. Will it last longer than the payback period (greenhouse plastic and pump parts wear out)? If you borrow, is the loan's yearly cost lower than the return, and can you repay before the item pays back? What if yields or prices are 20% lower than you hoped? Use cautious numbers, ask the supplier for farmers who already use it, and talk to a trusted adviser before you buy. This course explains the method; it does not tell you what to buy.
Step by step:
- Write the full cost: item, delivery, installation, training.
- Estimate extra income per year, using cautious yields and prices.
- Subtract extra running costs to get extra net income per year.
- Payback = cost / extra net income per year.
- Simple return = extra net income / cost x 100.
- Check life of the item, loan cost and a 20% worse case; write your decision.
Words to know:
- Investment: money spent now on something that should earn more later.
- Extra net income: the extra money an investment brings in each year minus its extra running costs.
- Payback period: how many years it takes for the extra net income to pay back what you spent: cost / extra net income per year.
- Simple return: extra net income per year as a percentage of the cost.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya (licensed banks, microfinance banks and digital credit providers)
- Central Bank of Nigeria (licensed banks and microfinance banks)
- BCEAO, Central Bank of West African States (rules for banks and microfinance in XOF countries)
Try it now: Final task: make your farm cost and investment sheet. For one enterprise, include fixed and variable costs, cost per unit, one month of expense tracking, a 12-month cash-flow plan with shortfall months marked, break-even price and yield, and the payback period and simple return of one investment, with your decision and why.
You can now judge whether an investment will pay back, using payback period, simple return and a check of the risks.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Costs sorted and cost per unit Costs are missing or mixed up, or the cost per unit is wrong or missing. Every cost is marked fixed or variable, depreciation is included, and the cost per unit is correct. Fixed costs are shared fairly between enterprises and family labour is valued at the local day rate. Expense tracker Fewer than half the days are recorded, or there are no category totals. One month of expenses with all columns, totalled by category and enterprise, matching cash and mobile money. Also names the biggest category and one realistic way to cut it. Cash-flow plan Months are missing or closing balances are not carried forward. Twelve months with correct opening and closing balances, shortfall months circled, an action for each. Actions are dated and costed, and the plan has been updated with one real month. Break-even Break-even price or yield is missing or wrong. Break-even price and yield are correct and compared with the expected price and yield. Also shows the safety margin and what happens if the yield falls by 20%. Investment decision No payback or return, or the decision has no reasons. Payback and simple return are correct and the decision gives at least two risks checked. Includes a 20% worse case, the item's life and the cost of any loan, with a clear yes, no or wait. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the sheet and check it again.

check.q: A cold store costs 200,000 and adds 50,000 extra net income a year. What is the payback period?
An item pays back in 6 years but the supplier says it lasts about 4 years. What does this tell you?
options: It will wear out before it pays back, so it is likely a loss
Payback does not matter if the item is new
You should borrow more to buy two
check.why: If the item wears out before payback, its extra income never covers its cost.
